verses.note: God calls the sign by the name of the covenant it signifies. Christian theology uses the same way of speaking for the sacraments, as when Jesus says of the cup that it is ‘the new covenant in my blood’ (Luke 22:20), and the traditions differ on how closely sign and reality are joined.

Paul calls circumcision ‘a seal of the righteousness’ Abraham had by faith before he was circumcised (Romans 4:11). The sign confirms a promise already received; it does not create Abraham's standing with God.

Christians have long connected circumcision with baptism because Colossians 2:11-12 links the two. Those who baptize infants see in Isaac's eighth-day circumcision a covenant sign given to a child before he could believe; those who baptize believers only hold that the New Testament sign follows faith and that the link in Colossians is spiritual rather than a pattern for infants. Both positions are held by faithful churches.

The covenant sign is not treated as optional ceremony. The scene shows that a sign God appoints carries real weight, and Christian readers have often drawn from it the seriousness of the signs God gives his people, whatever their view of how those signs relate to the covenant.

The verse creates a rite whose purpose is remembrance in the full biblical sense: each generation keeps the day as participants in the rescue, not only as heirs of its story. Jesus's words at the Supper, ‘Do this in remembrance of me’, draw on this vocabulary, and Christians differ over what that remembrance involves, from a memorial of Christ's death (Zwingli and the Baptist tradition) to a real sharing in his body and blood (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and Reformed traditions, each explaining the presence differently).

The rescued sufferer's feast shared with the poor became, for many Christian readers, a picture of the Lord's Supper. Augustine, in his Expositions of the Psalms, read the eating of the poor and of the rich (verse 29) in that light. The psalm itself describes the Old Testament thanksgiving meal; the link is typological.

Christians have long connected this verse with baptism. Those who hold a sacramental view (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and many Anglican and Reformed) see in baptism the sign and instrument of the cleansing Ezekiel promised. Those who hold a symbolic or ordinance view (Baptists and many free churches) see baptism as the public witness to a cleansing the Spirit has already done. Both read Ezekiel's water as God's own act of purification.

Christians read the verse differently. Catholic, Orthodox, and Lutheran theology, citing it with John 3:5 and Acts 2:38, teaches that God ordinarily gives new birth through baptism received in faith. Baptist and many Reformed and evangelical Christians read baptism as the expected public confession of a faith already given, and point to the verse's own second half, which condemns unbelief alone. All sides should remember that the verse belongs to the disputed ending.

Christians differ on whether this meal is the Lord's Supper. Catholic, Orthodox, and many Anglican and Lutheran interpreters read it as eucharistic, pointing to the verbs of 22:19 and to ‘the breaking of bread’ in Acts 2:42. Many evangelical interpreters see an ordinary evening meal in which Jesus' familiar gesture gives him away. Both readings agree that Christ makes himself known at the table.

Christians read the water differently, and each reading has long standing. Most church fathers, and the Catholic, Orthodox, and Lutheran traditions, see a reference to baptism as the means by which the Spirit gives new birth. Calvin, in his commentary, took water and Spirit as one thing, the Spirit who cleanses like water, and many Reformed and Baptist interpreters follow him in reading Ezekiel 36 behind the verse. Ben Witherington (New Testament Studies 35, 1989) argued that water means physical birth, so that one must be born both naturally and spiritually; others see John the Baptist's baptism of repentance. The text does not settle the question by itself, and the church has not agreed on it.

The verse ties baptism to forgiveness and to the Spirit, and the traditions read the tie differently: as the means through which God grants both (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran), as the appointed moment of forgiveness for a penitent believer (Stone-Campbell churches), as the sign and seal joined to what it signifies (Reformed), or as the commanded public sign of a forgiveness received by repentance and faith (Baptist and many evangelicals). The chapter note sets these out; each tradition affirms that forgiveness is God's free gift through Christ.

‘The breaking of the bread’ may mean the Lord's Supper, the common meal, or both, since in the earliest church the Supper was eaten within a meal (1 Corinthians 11:20-26). Luke used the phrase for the risen Jesus being known in the breaking of bread (Luke 24:35).
